name: Cortexin

b.x: Over 200 published studies and 25+ years of clinical use across Russia and CIS countries. That's the evidence base behind Cortexin, a lyophilized polypeptide fraction extracted from the cerebral cortex of young cattle or pigs through acid extraction and purification at the Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology in St. Petersburg. The preparation belongs to the Khavinson peptide bioregulator class. Short-chain peptides under 10 kDa cross neuronal membranes and interact with chromatin, restoring expression of neurotrophic factors like BDNF and NGF. The result is a dual action: neuroprotection during acute injury plus longer-term neuroplasticity support through gene regulation. Clinical applications span ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, chronic cerebrovascular insufficiency, and pediatric neurodevelopmental conditions. In acute ischemic stroke, a Russian multicenter placebo-controlled trial of 272 patients [1] found two 10-day courses worked best alongside standard therapy. In chronic cerebral ischemia, an RCT (n=189) [2] found dose-dependent benefits at 20 mg/day, and the authors reported good tolerability. In the community, Cortexin occupies a quiet niche. Reddit mentions total roughly 20 to 40 threads. Users who try it consistently describe the same pattern: minimal subjective effects during the 10-day injection course, with cognitive clarity, improved memory consolidation, and mild anxiolytic quality emerging 1 to 4 weeks after the last injection. A meaningful minority reports zero effect. Access is the practical barrier; authentic GEROPHARM product requires cold-chain shipping from Russia. A 2022 Western meta-analysis [3] rated the overall evidence certainty as low to very low.

Cortexin operates through multiple pathways because it's a polypeptide complex, not a single molecule. The primary mechanism centers on tissue-specific bioregulation at the genomic level. Short-chain peptides in the 1 to 10 kDa range cross cell membranes and interact with promoter regions of genes encoding BDNF and NGF. This upregulation of neurotrophin expression promotes neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and axonal regeneration. At the receptor level, Cortexin shifts the balance between glutamatergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition. Under ischemic conditions, it reduces pathological glutamate release and attenuates NMDA receptor-mediated calcium influx. That limits excitotoxic neuronal death, the primary cause of irreversible damage during stroke. Electrophysiological studies confirm normalization of cortical bioelectrical activity and improved interhemispheric coherence on EEG. Direct antioxidant properties round out the profile. Cortexin scavenges reactive oxygen species and boosts endogenous antioxidant enzymes including superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase. Lipid peroxidation in neuronal membranes drops, preserving membrane integrity during oxidative stress. Additional downstream effects include stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential, caspase-3 downregulation (reducing apoptotic signaling), and modulation of IL-1beta and TNF-alpha in injured tissue.
Cortexin benefits center on neuroprotection, neurological recovery, and delayed-onset cognitive improvement across clinical and community settings.
Stroke recovery support: a Russian multicenter, placebo-controlled trial in 272 acute stroke patients reported benefit from adding Cortexin to standard care [1]. Two 10-day courses worked best.

Dose-dependent recovery in chronic cerebral ischemia: 20 mg once daily IM beat 10 mg on neurological symptoms, fatigue and sleep. The multicenter RCT split 189 patients into 20 mg, 10 mg and basic-treatment groups [2].
Cognitive clarity and memory consolidation are the most consistently reported community benefits; effects emerge 1 to 4 weeks post-course and persist 6 to 10 weeks before fading.
EEG normalization and improved cortical bioelectrical activity documented in clinical studies, with better interhemispheric coherence tracked across treatment courses.

Pediatric use in children with speech delay, ADHD, or after-effects of perinatal brain injury. A Russian multicenter study treated 635 children aged 3 to 7 with one 10-injection course [4]. It compared scores before and after treatment, with no placebo group, and reported better attention, memory and thinking.
Reduced post-traumatic epilepsy risk following TBI, with improved Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at follow-up in traumatic brain injury studies.

Evidence base is large (200+ papers) but predominantly Russian-language with limited independent replication. Best evidence is in acute stroke (multicenter placebo-controlled trial, n=272) [1] and chronic cerebral ischemia (n=189) [2].
Key Study
PMID 24874316 (Aliferova et al. 2014): multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Cortexin in 272 patients with acute ischemic stroke; two 10-day courses gave the best therapeutic effect.
Limitations

Predominantly Russian-language literature; minimal independent Western replication; polypeptide complex (not single molecule) limits PK/PD characterization; evidence certainty rated low-to-very-low in the only Western meta-analysis (PMID 36324709).
Community Experience
Community rates Cortexin as a subtle, delayed-onset cognitive enhancer rather than an acute nootropic.
Community dosing: 10 mg IM once daily × 10 days; some users run 10 mg BID (20 mg/day)
Responder rate is variable: a meaningful minority reports no effect. Most prized for post-TBI recovery and general neuroplasticity rather than performance optimization.

Community confidence in effects is weaker than the clinical trial data would suggest.

b.x: Cortexin ships as a lyophilized powder in 5 mg or 10 mg vials. You'll reconstitute each vial with 1 to 2 mL of sterile water for injection right before use. Don't store the reconstituted solution; use it immediately. For a 10 mg vial reconstituted with 1 mL sterile water: you get 10 mg/mL concentration. Draw up 100 units (the full 1.0 mL) on a U100 insulin syringe for a 10 mg dose. For the 5 mg beginner dose from a 10 mg vial, draw 50 units (0.5 mL). For a 5 mg vial with 1 mL water, the full syringe is your dose. The non-obvious thing most beginners miss: you won't feel much during the 10-day course. Peak effects show up 1 to 4 weeks after the last injection. Evaluating at Day 10 is the single most common mistake; give it a full month before judging. If the injection hurts, switch your diluent from sterile water to 0.5% procaine solution (unless you have a local anesthetic allergy). Deep IM injection into deltoid or gluteal muscle, rotated daily, minimizes site reactions. Cold-chain matters; inspect the powder on arrival. It should be white to off-white. Discard if discolored, clumped, or if the vial seal is broken.
Cycling Protocol

Standard Russian protocol: 10-day treatment course (daily IM injections), repeated 2-4 times per year with at least 3-month intervals between courses. Acute conditions may use two courses back-to-back with a 10-day break.
Cortexin Cycle

Cortexin cycling follows a pulsed bioregulatory model: a 10-day injection course triggers a wave of BDNF/NGF gene expression and neurotrophic factor release that continues and matures for 4–8 weeks post-course. The 3-month minimum interval allows the full neurotrophic response to consolidate before the next stimulation. Running courses more frequently is not validated and may produce diminishing returns as the gene regulatory pathway requires recovery time. The interval also allows detection of any delayed adverse reactions and practical monitoring of cumulative benefit.
Effects from previous course have fully expressed and are beginning to fade (typically 6–10 weeks post-course)
Neurological or cognitive baseline has stabilized since last course
No persistent injection site reactions or allergic symptoms from prior course
Minimum 3 months elapsed since last course completion

Remove one Cortexin vial (10 mg) from refrigerator storage (2 to 8 degrees C). Allow to reach room temperature for 2 to 3 minutes. Inspect the lyophilized powder; it should be white to off-white with no discoloration or clumping.

Using a 3 mL syringe with a drawing needle (18 to 21 gauge), draw 1 mL of sterile water for injection or 0.5% procaine solution. Inject the diluent slowly down the side of the vial. Gently swirl until fully dissolved. Do not shake.

Swap to a 25 to 27 gauge intramuscular needle Draw the full 100 units (1.0 mL) from the vial. This equals your 10 mg dose. For a 5 mg dose from a 5 mg vial reconstituted with 1 mL, draw the full 100 units.
Choose your injection site: deltoid (upper arm) or gluteal muscle (upper outer quadrant of the buttock). Clean the area with an alcohol swab.
Insert the needle at a 90-degree angle into the muscle Inject slowly over 1 to 2 minutes. Slow injection reduces pain and improves absorption.
Withdraw the needle, apply gentle pressure with a cotton pad. Rotate injection sites daily across the 10-day course.
Inject every morning for 10 consecutive days Morning timing is preferred to avoid potential sleep disturbances. Repeat the 10-day course every 3 to 6 months.
Discard any remaining reconstituted solution Do not store or reuse.
Pediatric dosing: children under 20 kg receive 0.5 mg/kg/day, not exceeding 10 mg total.
Works With
Cerebrolysin

Most common Cortexin combination in Russian clinical neurology and the Western community. Complementary neuropeptide complexes: Cerebrolysin (whole-brain porcine extract) and Cortexin (cortex-specific bovine/porcine extract) are believed to have additive neurotrophic effects. Both run as 10-day IM courses, often simultaneously.
10 mg Cortexin IM + Cerebrolysin 5–10 mL IM/IV daily × 10 days
Semax

Semax (synthetic ACTH analogue, nasal or SC) provides acute cognitive activation while Cortexin provides sustained neurotrophic baseline support. Stack used in the community for general cognitive enhancement; Semax is taken daily, Cortexin in 10-day courses.
Semax 300–600 mcg intranasal daily during and after Cortexin course
Selank

Selank (anxiolytic/nootropic tetrapeptide) combined with Cortexin for anxiety reduction alongside neuroprotection. Community reports a combined anxiolytic and neuroplasticity benefit. Selank is taken daily, Cortexin in 10-day courses.
Selank 300 mcg intranasal BID during and after Cortexin course
Pinealon

Both are Khavinson-class peptide bioregulators. Pinealon (EDR tripeptide, pineal-specific) + Cortexin (cortex neuropeptides) stacked for broader bioregulatory coverage. Seen in Khavinson Institute multi-bioregulator protocols.
Avoid
Other CNS-active peptides (simultaneous courses)

Additive neurostimulatory effects possible when stacking multiple neuropeptide complexes simultaneously. No formal interaction data exists. Running Cortexin and Cerebrolysin at the same time is common practice, but adding a third CNS-active peptide complex (e.g., Selank + Semax + Cortexin + Cerebrolysin all at once) increases monitoring complexity without validated safety data.
Procaine/novocaine diluent (in patients with local anesthetic allergy)

Cortexin is sometimes reconstituted with 0.5% procaine to reduce injection pain. Contraindicated in patients with known allergy to local anesthetics (procaine, lidocaine, amide-class). Use sterile water for injection as the safe default diluent.

Prion-related concerns get the most attention from Western users, so start there. Cortexin is derived from bovine or porcine cerebral cortex tissue. The preparation's strict molecular weight cutoff (under 10 kDa) excludes prion-sized proteins, and no prion transmission cases have been documented in 25+ years of clinical use across millions of treatment courses in Russia and CIS countries. The risk is theoretical but not zero, and it's the primary hesitancy factor for users outside the CIS region. Allergic reactions are the most clinically relevant safety concern. Because the preparation contains animal-derived proteins, hypersensitivity responses including local urticaria and skin rash have been reported, primarily in patients with known sensitivity to bovine or porcine proteins. Anaphylaxis is rare but possible. Individuals with severe allergy history to bovine or porcine proteins should not use Cortexin. Injection site pain is common with IM administration. Reconstituting with 0.5% procaine (novocaine) solution instead of sterile water reduces this substantially, but procaine carries its own contraindication: patients with known allergy to local anesthetics (procaine, lidocaine, amide-class) must use sterile water only. Psychomotor agitation and sleep disturbances occur during the first few days of some treatment courses. These are transient and self-resolving, typically clearing by Day 4 to 5. Moving the injection to morning administration prevents most sleep disruption. Transient headache and dizziness shortly after administration are the most commonly noted side effects in clinical literature. Adverse event rates in RCTs were comparable to placebo. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: insufficient safety data exists. This is a contraindication. Known hypersensitivity to Cortexin, glycine, or other excipients is also a hard stop. When to stop: any sign of allergic reaction (rash, urticaria, facial swelling, respiratory distress). When to see a doctor: anaphylactic symptoms, persistent injection site infection, or psychomotor agitation that doesn't resolve after Day 3 to 4 of a course.
Common Issues & Solutions

No effect after first course: Cortexin effects are delayed: peak benefit emerges 1–4 weeks post-course, not during. Users who assess at Day 10 routinely miss the response window. Evaluate at 3–4 weeks post-course.

Injection site pain: Switch diluent from sterile water to 0.5% procaine solution (if no local anesthetic allergy). Ensure deep IM injection technique; superficial injection increases pain. Rotate sites each day.
Psychomotor agitation or sleep disruption (Days 1–3): Transient and well-documented. Move injection to morning if administering in the evening. Usually self-resolves by Day 4–5.

Vial received warm (cold-chain failure): Lyophilized powder requires 2–8°C storage. If received at room temperature for >24–48 hours, efficacy may be compromised. Verify the source uses a cold-chain guarantee with insulated packaging and ice packs.

Diminishing returns with repeated courses: Clinical data shows progressive improvement across courses in chronic conditions; in healthy users, benefit may plateau. If no additional benefit after 3–4 courses per year, consider spacing courses further apart or switching to a single annual course.

Cortexin: Product Quality medium risk

Cortexin is an animal-derived polypeptide complex requiring rigorous cold-chain maintenance. The authentic Russian product (GEROPHARM, St. Petersburg) is pharmaceutical-grade and well-standardized. Risk arises from: (1) cold-chain integrity during gray-market shipping; (2) difficulty authenticating product source outside Russia; (3) theoretical (unconfirmed) prion risk from bovine/porcine CNS tissue: mitigated by <10 kDa molecular weight cutoff that excludes prion-sized proteins.
Authentic Cortexin requires cold-chain shipping (ice packs and insulated packaging).
Authenticate packaging: genuine GEROPHARM Cortexin vials have holographic security labels; inspect packaging for Russian-language regulatory markings.
Inspect lyophilized powder appearance on receipt: should be white to off-white powder; discard if discolored, clumped, or if vial seal is compromised.
Do not accept or use vials received at room temperature for extended periods; lyophilized peptide complexes degrade faster than single-peptide products.
Confirm manufacturing batch number traceable to GEROPHARM; unbranded "Cortexin" from unverified Chinese or Indian sources has no traceable manufacturer.

Cortexin has been registered and approved in the Russian Federation since 1999 for a range of neurological indications including ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and cognitive disorders. It holds pharmaceutical registration across multiple CIS countries. No FDA approval exists. Cortexin has not been submitted for regulatory review in the United States, EU, UK, or any Western regulatory jurisdiction. It is classified as a research compound outside the CIS region. Cortexin is not on FDA's compounding lists. It appears in no 503A or 503B category (May 14, 2026; March 21, 2025) and not in 21 CFR 216.23. Customs enforcement on personal imports varies by country. For athletes: Cortexin is not named on WADA's 2026 Prohibited List. Its S0 class covers substances with no current approval by any government health authority. Cortexin holds Russian registration, so S0 does not reach the registered product. Competition-tested athletes should still verify current WADA guidance before use. Authentic Cortexin is manufactured by GEROPHARM in Russia. Holographic security labels and Russian-language regulatory markings identify the genuine product. Unbranded product has no traceable manufacturer. This content is for informational and research purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before using any peptide product.
Evidence grade: Approved outside the US (Peptide Evidence Gap, October 2026)

faqs.q: How is Cortexin different from Cerebrolysin?
faqs.a: Both are animal-brain polypeptide extracts used in Russian neurology, but Cerebrolysin is derived from porcine brain tissue broadly while Cortexin is extracted specifically from the cerebral cortex with a stricter <10 kDa molecular weight cutoff. Cerebrolysin has slightly more Western clinical trial data, including some independent European studies. Both are IM-only with similar 10-day course structures.

faqs.q: Does Cortexin need to be refrigerated?
faqs.a: Yes. The lyophilized powder is stored at 2–8°C for up to 3 years in original packaging. Once reconstituted with sterile water or 0.5% procaine solution, it must be used immediately. No storage of reconstituted solution is recommended.

faqs.q: Can you feel Cortexin working during the 10-day course?
faqs.a: Many users report minimal subjective effects during the course itself, with effects emerging in the 1–4 weeks post-course as neurotrophic changes accumulate. This is the established pattern: Days 1–7 are largely symptom-free, with peak effects at Day 8–10 and post-course continuation.

Yes, in one multicenter RCT (Fedin 2018, PMID 30335070). It split 189 adults with chronic cerebral ischemia into three groups: 69 got 20 mg IM once daily, 68 got 10 mg once daily, and 52 got basic treatment only. Courses ran 10 days and repeated after 6 months. The 20 mg group improved more on neurological symptoms, fatigue and sleep, and the authors reported good tolerability. The aggressive tier follows that schedule, 20 mg once daily; the trial did not test 10 mg twice daily or enroll healthy adults.

Theoretical, but Cortexin's strict <10 kDa molecular weight cutoff means prion proteins (which are much larger) are excluded from the preparation. No prion transmission cases have been documented from Cortexin in 25+ years of use across millions of treatment courses in Russia and CIS countries.

faqs.q: What is the recommended Cortexin dosage?
faqs.a: Cortexin dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 5 mg daily, moderate users at 10 mg daily, and aggressive protocols use 20 mg daily.
Cortexin typically comes in 5mg or 10mg vials. Mix it with Sterile Water for Injection, not bacteriostatic water, using the volume the product's directions give for your vial size.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Cortexin?
faqs.a: The half-life of Cortexin is ~1-3 hours (estimated, polypeptide complex). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.
